claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary alloy has a lower effective stacking-fault energy than its equiatomic quaternary and ternary FCC subsets.
The quinary alloy's lower stacking-fault energy is caused by its greater elemental complexity.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes deformation twinning rather than dislocation slip.
Enhanced deformation twinning contributes to greater strain hardening.
Enhanced twinning alters failure behavior relative to the quaternary and ternary alloys.
All compared alloys can be prepared as single-phase FCC materials with identical thermomechanical histories.
Effective stacking-fault energy controls the balance between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Complex interatomic interactions among the five constituents lower the effective stacking-fault energy of the quinary alloy.
Deformation twins act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Twin-mediated obstruction of dislocations enhances strain hardening.
Reduced constituent diversity in the quaternary and ternary alloys produces higher stacking-fault energy.
Reduced constituent diversity in the quaternary and ternary alloys produces lower twinning activity.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have higher stacking-fault energies.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower deformation-twin densities.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have reduced strain-hardening capacity.
The proposed relationship applies under room-temperature, low-strain-rate deformation of single-phase FCC alloys with microstructural heterogeneities minimized.
Failure to observe statistically distinguishable stacking-fault energies or twinning frequencies between the quinary and lower-order alloys would falsify the proposed complexity-driven mechanism.
